story: At the Mat-Su Sentinel's October 4th candidate forum in Palmer, 57 of 112 phone respondents said the state should outlaw large AI and data center development, while DNR weighs a 19,950-acre conveyance to AIDEA near Houston that could host data centers

claims.claim: The Mat-Su Sentinel held its Flip the Script State Edition candidate forum on Sunday, October 4th, at the Glenn Massey Theater in Palmer.
claims.verbatim: held Sunday at the Glenn Massey Theater in Palmer
claims.notes: The date comes from the photo caption on the same page: 'Candidates and residents attend Mat-Su Sentinel's Flip the Script: State Edition event on Oct. 4, 2026.' Calendar check: October 4th, 2026 is a Sunday. The Sentinel organized the forum, so this is the organizer's own account (marked primary). Article by Mat-Su Sentinel Staff, published October 9th, inside the window.

claims.claim: The State Edition forum drew about 200 residents.
claims.verbatim: about 200 residents and 22 candidates
claims.notes: This is the organizer's own approximate headcount. Keep 'about'. Response counts per question in the results PDF range from 92 to 133, which fits roughly 200 attendees given that not everyone answered every question.

claims.claim: 22 candidates for the Alaska Legislature attended the State Edition forum.
claims.verbatim: about 200 residents and 22 candidates
claims.notes: Single source, but it is the organizer.

claims.claim: The forum's candidates were running for Alaska House Districts 25 through 30 and Senate Districts M and O.
claims.verbatim: candidates for Alaska House Districts 25 through 30 and Senate Districts M and O.
claims.notes: The results PDF also lists Senate District N among respondents (28 people). Respondents came from N even though the article names only M and O for candidates.

claims.claim: Audience members at the forum answered live polling questions on their phones.
claims.verbatim: Audience members used their phones to respond to live polling questions
claims.notes: The article calls this 'live audience polling' and never says it is unscientific. The Sentinel also notes that residents 'were not asked their party affiliation'. The deck must describe it as a self-selected room of people who came to a candidate forum, not as a poll of Mat-Su.

claims.claim: The live polling results appeared on screen in real time.
claims.verbatim: with the results appearing on screen in real time.
claims.notes: Because results were visible in real time, later respondents could see earlier answers. This is a further reason not to treat the counts as independent opinion measurement.

claims.claim: The forum format did not ask candidates to debate one another.
claims.verbatim: Rather than asking candidates to debate one another or respond to a series of questions
claims.notes: The fetch paraphrase says candidates introduced themselves and listened. Only the verbatim fragment above is confirmed, so 'the audience answered and candidates listened' should be lightly hedged.

claims.claim: A second Sentinel forum, the Borough Edition, was held Thursday, October 8th, at the Palmer Depot.
claims.verbatim: held Thursday at the Palmer Depot, brought together about 150 residents
claims.notes: The date is from the photo caption 'Flip the Script: Borough Edition event on Oct. 8, 2026.' October 8th, 2026 is a Thursday. The Borough Edition had its own results PDF, which was not fetched. Use no Borough Edition counts.

claims.claim: The Borough Edition forum brought together about 150 residents.
claims.verbatim: brought together about 150 residents and most candidates
claims.notes: Approximate. Keep 'about'.

claims.claim: The State Edition asked the room whether the state should restrict large AI and data center development in areas like Mat-Su, and 112 responses were recorded.
claims.verbatim: Should the state restrict large AI/data center development in areas like Mat-Su? ... 14 112 112
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel (Flip the Script State Edition results)
claims.notes: Confirmed by WebFetch of https://r.jina.ai/ on the PDF URL. The counts were also read from the showrunner's pypdf extraction at /home/user/alaskaaicarousels/out/2026-10-12/scouts/matsu_state_pdf.txt (scripts/fetch_pdf_text.py). The verbatim combines the question line with the printed total line, and '...' marks an elision. The three options sum exactly to 112 (57+8+47), matching the printed total. The PDF carries no date of its own. The Oct 9th article links it as '2026 Flip the Script State Edition Results.pdf', and the file path is /2026/10/. A respondent count, not a sample of Mat-Su.

claims.claim: 57 of the 112 forum respondents chose to outlaw large AI and data center development entirely.
claims.verbatim: Outlaw them entirely 57
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel (Flip the Script State Edition results)
claims.suggested_phrasing: 57 of 112 people who answered on their phones at the Sentinel's candidate forum chose 'Outlaw them entirely'
claims.notes: 57/112 = 50.9 percent. Confirmed via r.jina.ai and the pypdf extraction. The forum audience was self-selected and answered with results visible on screen, so this is not a scientific poll and must never be written as 'Mat-Su residents want' or 'half of Mat-Su'.

claims.claim: 47 of the 112 forum respondents chose to allow large AI and data center development but with strict regulations.
claims.verbatim: Allow them, but with strict regulations47
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel (Flip the Script State Edition results)
claims.suggested_phrasing: 47 in the room chose 'Allow them, but with strict regulations'
claims.notes: 47/112 = 42.0 percent. The verbatim is the pypdf extraction string, which has no space before 47. The r.jina.ai render reads 'Allow them, but with strict regulations': 47. Self-selected forum audience.

claims.claim: 8 of the 112 forum respondents chose to allow large AI and data center development without restriction.
claims.verbatim: No, allow them 8
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel (Flip the Script State Edition results)
claims.suggested_phrasing: 8 in the room chose 'No, allow them'
claims.notes: 8/112 = 7.1 percent. The option text is 'No, allow them', answering the question 'Should the state restrict...'. Self-selected forum audience.

claims.claim: The Sentinel reported that about half of forum participants favored prohibiting large AI and data center developments.
claims.verbatim: About half favored prohibiting large artificial intelligence and data center developments
claims.suggested_phrasing: according to the Sentinel, about half of those who answered at its forum favored prohibiting them
claims.notes: Consistent with C11 (57/112 = 50.9 percent). The same article adds 'most of the remaining respondents supported strict regulations.'

claims.claim: 69 forum respondents chose no state subsidy for a gas pipeline, against a printed question total of 127.
claims.verbatim: $0, no state subsidy 69
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel (Flip the Script State Edition results)
claims.suggested_phrasing: 69 in the room chose '$0, no state subsidy'
claims.notes: TOTAL MISMATCH. The options are $0 69, up to $5B 19, up to $10B 17, $20B or more 13, and state pays the whole thing up to $60B 7. They sum to 125, but the PDF prints 127. The Sentinel's '55% opposed' (C16) matches 69/125 = 55.2 percent, while 69/127 = 54.3 percent. Prefer the raw count '69' and avoid the denominator, or cite the Sentinel's 55 percent with attribution. Self-selected audience.

claims.claim: The Sentinel reported that 55 percent of forum participants opposed using any state money to build a natural gas pipeline.
claims.verbatim: 55% opposed using any state money to build a natural gas pipeline
claims.suggested_phrasing: 55 percent of those answering at the forum, according to the Sentinel
claims.notes: Derived by the Sentinel from 69/125 (the option sum), not the printed 127. See C15.

claims.claim: Asked which energy source Alaska should prioritize, 52 forum respondents chose both natural gas and renewables equally.
claims.verbatim: Both equally 52
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel (Flip the Script State Edition results)
claims.notes: TOTAL MISMATCH. The options (gas pipeline 51, renewables 28, both 52) sum to 131, but the PDF prints 133. Use the raw counts and not percentages. Self-selected audience.

claims.claim: 51 forum respondents said Alaska should prioritize natural gas from a pipeline.
claims.verbatim: Natural gas (pipeline) 51
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel (Flip the Script State Edition results)
claims.notes: Same question as C17. Printed total 133 against an option sum of 131.

claims.claim: 28 forum respondents said Alaska should prioritize renewables such as wind, solar, geothermal and tidal.
claims.verbatim: Renewables (wind, solar, geothermal, tidal)28
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel (Flip the Script State Edition results)
claims.notes: Same question as C17. Printed total 133 against an option sum of 131.

claims.claim: 52 of 105 forum respondents opposed state funding for the West Susitna Access Road.
claims.verbatim: Do you support state funding for the West Susitna Access Road? ... No 52
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel (Flip the Script State Edition results)
claims.suggested_phrasing: 52 of 105 in the room said no
claims.notes: Yes 32, No 52, and 'Only if it can be shown to pay for itself' 21. These sum exactly to the printed 105. 52/105 = 49.5 percent, which the article rounds to 'half opposed state funding for the proposed West Susitna Access Road.' '...' in the verbatim marks an elision.

claims.claim: 101 of 111 forum respondents said Alaska residents fishing for personal use and subsistence should get priority when fish runs are limited.
claims.verbatim: Alaska residents (personal use/subsistence)101
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel (Flip the Script State Edition results)
claims.notes: Options sum exactly to the printed 111 (2+101+2+6). Corroborated by the article: '101 of 111 respondents saying Alaska residents fishing for personal use'. Self-selected audience.

claims.claim: House District 25 supplied the largest group of State Edition respondents, with 29 people.
claims.verbatim: House District 2529
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel (Flip the Script State Edition results)
claims.notes: In the pypdf string, district number and count run together ('House District 2529' = HD25, 29). The r.jina.ai render separates them as HD25 29, HD26 18, HD27 12, HD28 11, HD29 21, HD30 12. TOTAL MISMATCH: these sum to 103, but the PDF prints 104. Only about 104 of the roughly 200 attendees answered this question, which shows that counts vary by question.

claims.claim: 53 State Edition respondents placed themselves in Senate District M, the largest Senate group in the room.
claims.verbatim: Senate District M53
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel (Flip the Script State Edition results)
claims.notes: Senate M 53, N 28 (printed 'Distirct' typo in source), O 38. TOTAL MISMATCH: these sum to 119, but the PDF prints 120. Low editorial value. Optional.

claims.claim: Alaska DNR proposed conveying approximately 19,950 acres of state land near Houston to the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority.
claims.verbatim: approximately 19,950 acres
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Natural Resources, Division of Mining, Land and Water
claims.notes: BACKGROUND, outside the window. Notice title is 'Proposed Land Conveyance to Alaska Industrial Development Export Authority near the city of Houston', published July 10th, 2026. The parcel lies 'approximately two miles north of Houston in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough.' Corroboration: ADN/AJOC says '20,000 acres', Alaska Public says '30 square miles' (about 19,200 acres), and KTNA says 'nearly 20,000 acres'. These are rounded and consistent. The notice itself does not mention data centers. That link comes from the AIDEA proposal as reported (C38).

claims.claim: The proposed AIDEA conveyance near Houston is filed under ADL 234762.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Natural Resources, Division of Mining, Land and Water
claims.notes: The same ADL appears on the extension notice id=224879. Background.

claims.claim: DNR's decision on the Houston conveyance was issued as a preliminary decision, which becomes the final finding and decision if no significant change is required.
claims.verbatim: will be issued as the Final Finding and Decision
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Natural Resources, Division of Mining, Land and Water
claims.notes: The notice refers to 'the complete Preliminary Decision' as an attachment. Neither notice names an individual decider. The senators' letter is addressed to Natural Resources Commissioner John Crowther (C33), but do not write 'Crowther will decide' unless sourced. The underlying conveyance is a 'noncompetitive public and charitable use conveyance' (notice 224431).

claims.claim: DNR extended the public comment period on the Houston conveyance to September 14th.
claims.verbatim: EXTENDED COMMENT PERIOD ENDS 5:00PM, MONDAY, SEPTEMBER14, 2026
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Natural Resources, Division of Mining, Land and Water
claims.notes: The original deadline on notice 224431 was 5 p.m. August 19th. The extension notice was published August 19th. Background.

claims.claim: DNR said it was reviewing more than 2,100 public comments on the proposed AIDEA land transfer.
claims.verbatim: along with more than 2,100 comments
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Journal of Commerce (Anchorage Daily News)
claims.suggested_phrasing: according to a DNR spokesperson quoted by the Alaska Journal of Commerce
claims.notes: DATE CORRECTION. The scout listed this as October 4th from the URL path, but the page shows 'September 28, 2026' by Iris Samuels, which is two days before the window opens. Treat it as background. The figure is a DNR spokesperson's count relayed by the paper, single-sourced.

claims.claim: A legal memo by Legislature attorney Alpheus Bullard warned that the AIDEA conveyance may raise legal issues.
claims.verbatim: "Without this analysis, the conveyance may raise legal issues," wrote Bullard.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Journal of Commerce (Anchorage Daily News)
claims.suggested_phrasing: a Legislature attorney wrote that the conveyance 'may raise legal issues' without further analysis
claims.notes: The memo itself was not fetched. The quote is verbatim on the AJOC page. Bullard's warning is conditional ('Without this analysis'), so do not drop the condition or state that the transfer is illegal. The Google News listing for an Alaska Beacon September 16th piece, 'Alaska senators question legality of state land transfer for possible Mat-Su data centers', independently describes the memo, but that page was not read.

claims.claim: Senate Resources Committee Chair Cathy Giessel signed a September 9th letter raising concerns about the AIDEA land transfer.
claims.verbatim: The letter, dated Sept. 9, is signed by Senate Resources Committee Chair Cathy Giessel, R-Anchorage.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Journal of Commerce (Anchorage Daily News)
claims.notes: The letter itself was not fetched. AJOC also reports that Giessel supports 'a moratorium on data center development until the state Legislature passes new laws.'

claims.claim: Five members of the Senate Resources Committee signed the September 9th letter on the AIDEA transfer.
claims.verbatim: Sen. Bill Wielechowski, D-Anchorage; Sen. Matt Claman, D-Anchorage;
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Journal of Commerce (Anchorage Daily News)
claims.notes: The page names Giessel (R-Anchorage) plus Bill Wielechowski, Matt Claman and Forrest Dunbar (all D-Anchorage) and Scott Kawasaki (D-Fairbanks), five in all. The count of five is our tally of the named signers. The page text read in full was not confirmed to contain the word 'five'.

claims.claim: The senators' letter asked Natural Resources Commissioner John Crowther to clarify whether the state could protect the public interest after the transfer.
claims.verbatim: Natural Resources Commissioner John Crowther to clarify whether the state is in a position
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Journal of Commerce (Anchorage Daily News)
claims.suggested_phrasing: the letter asks Commissioner John Crowther to clarify the state's position
claims.notes: The 'protect the public interest' completion comes from the fetch summary. Only the verbatim fragment is confirmed, so keep the claim close to the fragment.

claims.claim: As of late September, DNR had not issued a final decision on the AIDEA conveyance and said any final decision would address public, agency and legislative feedback.
claims.verbatim: Any final decision will address feedback from the public, agencies, and Legislature.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Journal of Commerce (Anchorage Daily News)
claims.suggested_phrasing: DNR has said any final decision will address the feedback, and none had been announced as of this run
claims.notes: This is a DNR spokesperson quote. Scout A separately reported ADL 234762 'still pending'. No final finding was found on DNR's public notice site in this check, but that site was not exhaustively searched.

claims.claim: The Mat-Su Borough Assembly unanimously approved a resolution formally opposing the state plan to transfer nearly 20,000 acres to AIDEA.
claims.verbatim: The Assembly unanimously approved the resolution during a regular meeting Tuesday.
claims.notes: The lead also says 'The Matanuska-Susitna Borough Assembly this week formally opposed a state plan to transfer nearly 20,000 acres'. The byline is Mat-Su Sentinel, published September 16th (a Wednesday), so 'Tuesday' means September 15th. That date is our calendar inference, and no page states 'September 15' outright. Write 'in mid-September' or 'on September 15th' only with that inference acknowledged. No vote count or resolution number is given. The resolution itself was not fetched. Background, outside the window.

claims.claim: The Assembly resolution called for industrial projects to go instead to land at Point MacKenzie or in the West Susitna.
claims.verbatim: It calls for such projects to instead be located on "more appropriate" land at Point MacKenzie or in the West Susitna.
claims.notes: Curly quotes are normalized to straight. The same article says the resolution 'does not specifically mention large-scale data centers'. Do not say the Assembly opposed data centers.

claims.claim: At an August 13th Houston City Council meeting, an ordinance to block data center construction within city limits failed 4 to 2.
claims.verbatim: failed 4-2, with council members Callie Courtney and Lisa Johansen voting yes.
claims.notes: The date fragment is 'Houston City Council meeting Aug. 13, 2026'. Byline Amy Bushatz, Mat-Su Sentinel, published on Alaska Public August 18th. Background. The ordinance failed, so write 'the council voted down a data center ban 4 to 2' rather than 'rejected'. Council member Jeffry Brasel was quoted as saying 'There was zero transparency.'

claims.claim: Houston City Council member Jeffry Brasel said there was zero transparency in the land transfer process.
claims.verbatim: There was zero transparency. They had made preliminary decisions before we made or even had a decision to make.
claims.notes: Named-person quote, verbatim per fetch. One-sided framing, so attribute it to Brasel explicitly.

claims.claim: The AIDEA proposal for the Houston parcel lists scalable data centers among possible uses, though AIDEA says no specific projects are proposed or approved.
claims.verbatim: scalable data centers,
claims.suggested_phrasing: a site that could include data centers, though AIDEA says none is proposed
claims.notes: The AIDEA disclaimer comes from the fetch summary of the same page. KTNA (C34 URL) also says the proposal lists 'scalable data centers'. AJOC describes 'a multi-use industrial and energy development district' that could include data centers. Never write that a data center is planned there.

claims.claim: Terra Energy leased 829 acres of University of Alaska land at Port MacKenzie.
claims.verbatim: Terra Energy has leased 829 acres of University of Alaska land.
claims.notes: By Tim Bradner and Amy Bushatz, October 6th, inside the window. Port MacKenzie is in the headline. The scout's '829.34 acres' is not on this page. The UA intent-to-lease notice (C41) lists four parcels of 369.34, 80, 60 and 320 acres, which sum to 829.34, but that notice does not name the lessee. Use '829 acres'. The article says Terra 'intends to lease for similar projects, including data centers' on nearby borough land, while UA's own information 'does not highlight data centers'.

claims.claim: Terra Energy signed a 20-year lease with the University of Alaska in late May.
claims.verbatim: Terra Energy signed a 20-year lease with UA in late May, according to university officials.
claims.notes: Attributed by the Sentinel to university officials.

claims.claim: The University of Alaska gave public notice on January 30th of its intent to lease four parcels of land near Point MacKenzie.
claims.verbatim: Intent to Lease Multiple Parcels of University of Alaska Land
claims.notes: Parcels MS.PM.0001 (369.34 acres), 0002 (80), 0003 (60) and 0004 (320), each 'more or less', for a total of 829.34 acres. They are described as 'near Point MacKenzie', and 0004 is 'west of Port MacKenzie'. The notice names no lessee and no term. The link to Terra rests on the Sentinel (C39) and the matching acreage. Background.

claims.claim: The U.S. Department of Energy selected Terra Energy Center Corporation for $89,000,000 in federal funding.
claims.verbatim: DOE Funding: $89,000,000
claims.notes: The DOE page is undated, so date_of_source is left blank and the retrieval date is recorded in retrieved. The project is titled 'Alaska Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage Coal Commissioning Project', Terra Energy Center Corporation (Anchorage, Alaska), under BAA DE-FOA-0003605. Corroboration: the Mat-Su Sentinel (C39 URL) says 'The company received an $89 million grant from the U.S. Department of Energy this summer.' A selection is not a disbursed award, so 'selected for' is the safe verb.

claims.claim: The DOE-selected Terra project covers engineering and design of a 1,250 MW coal-fired power plant with carbon capture in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough.
claims.verbatim: Project focusing on engineering and design of a 1,250 MW (target gross) nameplate-capacity, coal-fired baseload
claims.suggested_phrasing: a proposed 1,250 MW (target gross) coal plant; the DOE money is for engineering and design
claims.notes: The source page is undated; date_of_source is left blank and the retrieval date is recorded in retrieved. This is a target capacity for a proposed plant, not a built plant. The DOE text continues 'power facility with integrated CCUS, sited in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough of Southcentral Alaska' and says it would capture 'greater than 90%' of CO2, 'an estimated 8.26 million tonnes annually.' The Sentinel places the plant near Skwentna, with carbon piped more than 60 miles to Cook Inlet.

claims.claim: The Alaska Senate passed SB 250, a data center bill, 14 to 5 on reconsideration on May 16th.
claims.verbatim: (S) PASSED ON RECONSIDERATION Y14 N5 E1
claims.notes: Read via https://r.jina.ai/https://www.akleg.gov/basis/Bill/Detail/34?Root=SB%20250 because akleg is reachable through that reader. The first third-reading vote the same day was 'PASSED Y13 N5 E2', and reconsideration produced Y14 N5 E1. Corroborated by Alaska Public / Alaska Beacon September 21st ('voted 14-5 to pass a data center bill'). The version passed was CSSB 250(CRA). date_of_source is the last action date on the bill page.

claims.claim: SB 250 was heard and held in the House Community and Regional Affairs Committee on May 18th and did not pass the House before the session ended.
claims.verbatim: (H) Heard & Held -- Recessed to a Call of the Chair --
claims.notes: Referred to House CRA May 17th, heard May 18th, no later action. Alaska Public says 'the House did not act on it before the session ended'. BASIS shows a hearing, so prefer 'stalled in a House committee' over 'the House never took it up'. Sponsor Sen. Löki Tobin, D-Anchorage, per Alaska Public (C46).

claims.claim: SB 250 was sponsored by Sen. Löki Tobin of Anchorage and would have regulated data centers' use of utility electricity and required decommissioning plans.
claims.verbatim: voted 14-5 to pass a data center bill
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon via Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: The sponsor and the bill content are from the fetch summary of the article. The only confirmed verbatim fragment is the vote line. The BASIS fetch did not surface a sponsor field. Background (September 21st, James Brooks, Alaska Beacon).

claims.claim: Republican governor candidate Dave Bronson said he is a big believer in data centers.
claims.verbatim: I'm a big believer in data centers. I know that might be unpopular with some folks here.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon via Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: The apostrophe is normalized to straight (the page uses a curly one). He said it at a Commonwealth North forum. He also said 'There's a lot of money in data centers, but you've got to deal with the noise.' Background, outside the window. KTUU October 7th (Beacon) reportedly says only Bronson backs large data centers, but that page was not read.

claims.claim: Republican governor candidate Treg Taylor said of data centers that Alaska needs to embrace it.
claims.verbatim: I think we need to embrace it,
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon via Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: Background. The 'it' refers to data centers per the article ('he said of data centers').

claims.claim: Treg Taylor said data centers in Alaska should bring their own energy.
claims.verbatim: bring their own energy
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon via Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: He also said 'It doesn't have to drive up costs if you do it correctly.' Background.

claims.claim: Republican governor candidate Bernadette Wilson said she will never allow Alaska to be littered with hyperscale data centers.
claims.verbatim: I will never allow Alaska to be littered with hyperscale data centers that take our resources and spoil our lands.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon via Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: The statement was given by text message, according to the article. Background.

claims.claim: Democratic governor candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins said he supports a moratorium on data center development in Alaska until the Legislature passes a regulatory framework.
claims.verbatim: I support a moratorium on data center development in Alaska
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon via Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: VERBATIM LIMIT. Only 'I support a moratorium on data center development in Alaska' is confirmed character for character. The fuller quote reportedly continues 'until the Legislature can pass ... a comprehensive regulatory framework for that development in Alaska', but the fetch tool split it and contiguity is not proven. In quotation marks, use only the confirmed fragment and paraphrase the rest. Background.

claims.claim: Alaska's general election is on November 3rd.
claims.verbatim: General Election Day. Polls open from 7a.m. - 8p.m.
claims.notes: The calendar page is undated; date_of_source is left blank and the retrieval date is recorded in retrieved. Read via r.jina.ai. The calendar lists 11/03/2026 against that entry. The page's dash between the times is shown here as a hyphen. The calendar is undated, so date_of_source is the retrieval date. The scout-cited homepage returned 503 directly, and via r.jina.ai it does not show the election date. The calendar also lists 10/04/2026 as the registration deadline, the day of the forum.

claims.claim: Early and in-person absentee voting for the general election begins October 19th.
claims.verbatim: Voting begins October 19 for the 2026 General Election
claims.notes: The Division of Elections home page is undated; date_of_source is left blank and the retrieval date is recorded in retrieved. Read via r.jina.ai (the direct fetch returned 503). Corroborated on https://www.elections.alaska.gov/calendar/ at 10/19/2026 with 'Absentee In Person, EV, electronic transmission and Special Needs voting begins.' The homepage also gives an absentee by-mail application deadline of October 24th.

claims.claim: The Fairbanks North Star Borough Assembly voted 6 to 1 on August 27th for 2027 legislative priorities that include a moratorium on commercial data centers on municipal or state-owned land.
claims.verbatim: voted 6-1 in favor of adopting a set of legislative priorities for 2027
claims.notes: Optional context. Date fragment 'On Aug. 27.' The moratorium is 'pending the creation of standards for addressing community concerns'. Byline Alex Bengel, published September 29th, 4:38 p.m. AKDT. The URL path says 09/30. One day before the window, so background.

claims.claim: UAF's drone icing tower is formally called the Supercooled Water Experimental Arctic Tower, or SWEAT.
claims.verbatim: the Supercooled Water Experimental Arctic Tower, or SWEAT
claims.notes: By Rod Boyce, September 30th, inside the window. Operated by ACUASI (Alaska Center for Unmanned Aircraft Systems Integration). 'The tower can create various types of calibrated icing conditions.' Corroborated by DroneLife October 2nd.

claims.claim: The SWEAT ice tower stands about 16 feet tall.
claims.verbatim: It stands at about 16 feet
claims.notes: The 4.9 meter figure appears on DroneLife ('Standing about 16 feet (4.9 meters) tall in a fenced area behind the UAF Reichardt Building'), not on the UAF page.

claims.claim: Coda Consulting of Ottawa, Canada, built the SWEAT tower.
claims.verbatim: Coda Consulting of Ottawa, Canada, built the tower.
claims.notes: DroneLife credits Eyal Saiet with leading development. That does not conflict, since Saiet led development and Coda built it.

claims.claim: The SWEAT tower opened in early 2025.
claims.verbatim: It opened in early 2025.
claims.notes: Corroborated by DroneLife: 'the facility opened in early 2025.'

claims.claim: The SWEAT tower currently lacks a horizontal component for creating wind scenarios.
claims.verbatim: lacks a horizontal component for creating wind scenarios
claims.notes: DroneLife reports that Saiet hopes to expand the tower to serve fixed-wing drones. That is an aspiration, so hedge it if used.

claims.claim: UAF's aerospace engineering degree added a robotics track in 2026.
claims.verbatim: new in 2026 - robotics
claims.notes: The page uses an em dash, which is rendered here as a hyphen per house rule. The program offers four tracks (aeronautics, unmanned aircraft systems, space systems and astrodynamics) plus robotics. Corroborated by DroneLife: 'robotics, which launched in 2026.'

claims.claim: UAF's aerospace engineering degree program is entering its fourth academic year.
claims.verbatim: entering its fourth academic year
claims.notes: Corroborated by DroneLife: 'the UAF aerospace engineering degree program, now entering its fourth academic year.'

claims.claim: Enstar applied to the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission on September 17th to convert the nearly depleted Kenai Loop field into underground gas storage.
claims.verbatim: an underground natural gas storage reservoir and facility
claims.notes: THIRD story. By Kristen Nelson, October 11th. The filing date fragment is 'Sept. 17'. The article says the field is 'almost depleted', so do not write 'depleted' flat. The AOGCC filing was not fetched. Proposed storage service uses 'three existing wells, KL 1-1, KL 1-3 and KL 1-4'.

claims.claim: Enstar's reservoir simulation indicates a maximum working gas inventory of about 20.5 bcf at Kenai Loop.
claims.verbatim: reservoir simulation indicating a maximum working gas inventory of some 20.5 bcf
claims.suggested_phrasing: up to about 20.5 bcf of working gas under a conceptual nine-well plan
claims.notes: This is a simulated maximum under a conceptual nine-well plan, with 8 bcf of base gas. It is a projection, not a capacity.

claims.claim: AOGCC has tentatively scheduled a public hearing on Enstar's Kenai Loop storage application for November 12th.
claims.verbatim: AOGCC has tentatively scheduled a public hearing for Nov. 12 at 10 a.m.
claims.notes: Tentative. Hearing requests are due in writing by 4:30 p.m. October 20th ('Requests for the hearing must be in writing and filed with AOGCC by 4:30 p.m. Oct. 20.'). The AOGCC notice itself was not fetched, so this rests on the trade press only.

claims.notes: The 2026-10-11 date was the retrieval date, not a publication date; it is recorded in retrieved. Fetched by the showrunner.
